title: Chapter 11 Drill: Office Practice: Primary Care, Preventive Health, and Infections

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman asks about cancer risk. Her sister had breast cancer at age 38, and her mother had ovarian cancer. The family is of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. What is the best next step?
options: Annual mammography starting immediately with no further workup
Discussion of risk-reducing mastectomy before any testing
Referral for genetic counseling and consideration of testing
Annual CA-125 measurement and transvaginal ultrasonography
items.explanation: Early breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and Ashkenazi ancestry all point toward a possible BRCA variant, so counseling and testing come first and guide every later decision. Imaging alone skips the diagnosis that determines risk. Surgery should not be discussed as a plan before a variant is known. CA-125 with ultrasonography has not been shown to reduce ovarian cancer mortality.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a fasting glucose of 118 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c of 6.0 percent. She had gestational diabetes twice and has a body mass index of 36. What is the best recommendation?
options: An intensive lifestyle program, with metformin considered
Insulin therapy to normalize her glucose now
No treatment, because she does not have diabetes
A sulfonylurea at a low starting dose
items.explanation: She has prediabetes, with an A1c of 5.7 to 6.4 percent and fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL. Intensive lifestyle change lowers progression, and metformin is considered when risk is high, as with prior gestational diabetes or a body mass index of 35 or more. Insulin and sulfonylureas are for established diabetes and carry hypoglycemia risk. Doing nothing wastes a chance to prevent progression.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman reports two falls in the past six months. She lives alone, takes no sedatives, and walks slowly on timed testing. What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: High-dose daily vitamin D to prevent falls
A structured exercise program focused on balance and strength
A nightly sleep aid to improve rest
Daily calcium supplementation at a high dose
items.explanation: Exercise programs that train balance, gait, and strength are the intervention with the best evidence for preventing falls in community-dwelling older adults at risk. Vitamin D supplementation has not been shown to prevent falls in healthy older women. Sedatives add to fall risk and should be reduced, not started. Calcium supports bone health but does not address the underlying cause of a fall.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has home blood pressure readings averaging 134 over 84 mm Hg on two weeks of monitoring. She has no diabetes, kidney disease, or cardiovascular disease, and her calculated 10-year risk is 3 percent. What is the best management?
options: Start a thiazide diuretic today and recheck in a month
Start an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor at a low dose
Lifestyle changes with repeat assessment in 3 to 6 months
Start a beta blocker and add a diuretic if needed
items.explanation: These readings are stage 1 hypertension. Without diabetes, kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, or a 10-year risk of 7.5 percent or more, a trial of diet, exercise, weight control, and sodium reduction is appropriate before drugs. Medication would be started if the target is not reached after that interval. Beta blockers are not first-line agents for uncomplicated hypertension.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman at 12 weeks of gestation has a positive nucleic acid test for chlamydia at her first prenatal visit. She has no drug allergies. What is the preferred treatment?
options: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, then retest at 3 months
Azithromycin 1 g orally once, with a test of cure in 4 weeks
Levofloxacin 500 mg daily for 7 days with retest at delivery
Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once, with no later testing
items.explanation: Doxycycline and fluoroquinolones are avoided in pregnancy, so azithromycin as a single 1 g dose is preferred. A test of cure about 4 weeks after treatment is advised in pregnancy, and retesting at 3 months follows because reinfection is common. Ceftriaxone treats gonorrhea but not chlamydia, and skipping follow-up testing in a pregnant patient is incorrect.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman who smokes one pack daily says she is ready to quit and has failed using patches alone. Which single drug has the greatest evidence of effectiveness for quitting?
options: Varenicline taken daily for 12 weeks
Bupropion sustained release for 7 weeks
Nicotine gum used when cravings occur
Clonidine taken twice daily for a month
items.explanation: Among single agents, varenicline has the highest quit rates, and it is given for a standard 12-week course while the patient also receives counseling. Bupropion works but is less effective. Short-acting nicotine gum alone is weaker than combination replacement with a patch. Clonidine is a second-line option because of side effects, and it is not preferred for a motivated patient.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman says she keeps missing her pills and her partner has thrown some away and pressures her to become pregnant. Which method is the best option?
options: A daily progestin-only pill taken at night
A vaginal ring she inserts herself monthly
Condoms that her partner must agree to use
A contraceptive implant, which her partner cannot easily detect
items.explanation: Sabotaging contraception to force pregnancy is reproductive coercion, a form of violence. Methods that do not depend on daily action or on the partner, such as an implant or injection, protect her best, and the visit should include a safety assessment and resources. Pills, rings she can lose, and condoms that need his cooperation are all easy for a controlling partner to interfere with.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman reports the sudden onset of the most severe headache of her life that reached peak intensity within a minute. She has a long history of mild migraine. What is the best next step?
options: A triptan with nonsteroidal pain relief
Start propranolol for migraine prevention
Urgent neuroimaging
Reassurance and a follow-up call in one week
items.explanation: A thunderclap headache is a red flag for subarachnoid hemorrhage and other emergencies, and it requires immediate imaging, not routine migraine therapy, even in a patient with known migraine. A triptan could be harmful if the cause is vascular. Preventive drugs do nothing for an acute event. Reassurance with delayed follow-up risks missing a fatal bleed.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has had adequate cervical screening, with three consecutive negative cytology tests and no history of CIN2 or higher in the past 25 years. What is the recommendation?
options: Continue Pap tests every 3 years for life
Discontinue cervical cancer screening
Annual HPV testing
One colposcopy before stopping
items.explanation: Screening may stop at age 65 in women with adequate negative prior screening, defined as three consecutive negative cytology results or two negative cotests within 10 years, with the most recent in the last 5 years, and no history of CIN2 or higher. Lifelong testing offers little benefit and causes false positives. Annual testing and routine colposcopy are not indicated in low-risk women.

items.stem: A woman at 34 weeks of gestation visits the clinic in October and asks about respiratory syncytial virus protection for her newborn. She has had no other vaccines this pregnancy. What is the best recommendation?
options: Offer one dose of the vaccine now, in season
Offer it after delivery so that she is protected
Offer a live attenuated vaccine at the next visit
Advise that no pregnancy vaccine exists for the virus
items.explanation: A single dose of the maternal vaccine is recommended between 32 0/7 and 36 6/7 weeks during the seasonal period, so antibody crosses the placenta before birth. Postpartum vaccination would protect her but not the baby. The product is not a live vaccine, and live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy. A pregnancy option does exist, so saying otherwise is incorrect.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a pathogenic BRCA1 variant asks how her breasts should be monitored. She has had no cancer and has not had surgery. What is the best recommendation?
options: Mammography alone, repeated every two years from age 50
Yearly breast magnetic resonance imaging and mammography
Breast ultrasonography alone, performed twice each year
Clinical breast examination only, with no imaging studies
items.explanation: A carrier has a lifetime risk well above the 20 percent threshold at which annual magnetic resonance imaging is advised alongside mammography. Biennial mammography alone is the average-risk plan. Ultrasonography alone lacks adequate sensitivity for this population. Clinical examination without imaging does not detect early cancers, which is the goal of surveillance in carriers of a pathogenic variant.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman was treated for early syphilis with benzathine penicillin G six months ago. Her rapid plasma reagin titer has fallen from 1:64 to 1:16, and she has no symptoms. What does this indicate?
options: Treatment failure that needs three weekly doses
Neurosyphilis that requires a lumbar puncture
A need to retreat with doxycycline for 28 days
Adequate response; continue routine follow-up
items.explanation: A fourfold, or two dilution, decline in the nontreponemal titer within the follow-up period shows a response, so routine serologic follow-up continues. Treatment failure would be a failure to fall by that amount or a rise. A lumbar puncture is for neurologic, ocular, or otic findings. Retreatment is unwarranted when the titer is falling appropriately.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl comes to the office with her mother for her first gynecologic visit because of painful periods. She is not sexually active and has no pelvic pain between cycles. What is appropriate regarding examination?
options: Perform a speculum examination and cervical cytology
Perform a bimanual examination to exclude a mass
History and counseling; no pelvic examination needed
Defer all gynecologic visits until she turns 21
items.explanation: The first gynecologic visit is advised between ages 13 and 15, and for most adolescent concerns it consists of history, education, and counseling without an internal examination. Cervical screening does not begin before age 21, and a speculum is unnecessary. A bimanual examination adds little in a virginal adolescent with typical dysmenorrhea. Deferring all care until 21 misses the chance for prevention.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl has severe menstrual pain that has not improved after three months each of scheduled nonsteroidal drugs and a combined oral contraceptive. Pain is now present between periods. What is the next step?
options: Evaluate for endometriosis; consider laparoscopy
Double the nonsteroidal dose beyond labeled limits
Offer hysterectomy to end the pain
Stop all treatment and review again in a year
items.explanation: Pain that fails both first-line nonsteroidal drugs and hormonal therapy after about three months, especially when it begins to occur outside menses, suggests secondary dysmenorrhea such as endometriosis, and evaluation with possible laparoscopy is indicated. Exceeding labeled doses risks harm without benefit. Hysterectomy is inappropriate in an adolescent. Withholding treatment ignores progressive disease and lets pain and scarring advance.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has persistent depressed mood and fatigue throughout the month, with symptoms that become noticeably worse in the week before menses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder
Premenstrual syndrome without functional impairment
Bipolar II disorder with a luteal pattern
Depressive disorder with premenstrual exacerbation
items.explanation: Symptoms that are present throughout the cycle and merely worsen before menses indicate an underlying mood disorder with premenstrual exacerbation. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder requires symptoms confined to the luteal phase, with relief soon after bleeding starts and minimal symptoms the following week. Premenstrual syndrome is milder and does not impair function. Nothing in the history suggests mania.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman with chlamydial infection asks that the clinic not tell the health department because she wants privacy. What is the correct response?
options: Withhold the report unless she gives written consent
Explain that the infection is reportable and file the report
Report only if she is also pregnant
Report gonorrhea but never chlamydia
items.explanation: Chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and human immunodeficiency virus infection are reportable to the health department, and the clinician or laboratory completes the report even when the patient prefers privacy. Reports are handled confidentially for surveillance and partner services. Consent is not required, and pregnancy does not change the duty. Chlamydia is reportable just as gonorrhea is.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has a new partner and no symptoms. A vaginal swab for nucleic acid amplification is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis, and she is not pregnant. Which treatment is preferred?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly as a single dose
Metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose
Cefixime 800 mg orally as a single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
items.explanation: Doxycycline for 7 days is the preferred regimen for uncomplicated chlamydial infection in a nonpregnant patient. Ceftriaxone treats gonorrhea and has no role as sole therapy for chlamydia. Metronidazole covers trichomonas and anaerobes, not chlamydia. Cefixime is an oral cephalosporin with poor activity against chlamydia. Azithromycin is reserved mainly for pregnancy or when adherence is a concern.

items.stem: A 27-year-old transgender woman has started oral estradiol with spironolactone. Which risk should be specifically discussed at the start of therapy?
options: Erythrocytosis requiring phlebotomy
Menstrual bleeding with progressive cycle irregularity
Venous thromboembolism, highest with oral estrogen
Cervical cancer arising in the neovagina
items.explanation: Estrogen therapy raises the risk of venous thromboembolism, and the risk is greatest with oral formulations, so patients are counseled and transdermal routes may be preferred when risk is elevated. Erythrocytosis is a testosterone effect in transgender men. Transgender women do not menstruate. Screening needs differ for the neovagina, and cervical cancer does not arise there because there is no cervix.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has mucopurulent cervicitis. Nucleic acid testing for gonorrhea is positive, and chlamydia testing is pending. She weighs 70 kg and has no drug allergy. Which regimen is most appropriate today?
options: Ceftriaxone intramuscularly plus doxycycline for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly alone, with no second drug
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg as a single dose
Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose alone
items.explanation: Gonorrhea is treated with one intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone, and doxycycline is added when chlamydia has not been excluded because the two infections often coexist. Ceftriaxone alone is appropriate only once chlamydia is ruled out. Quinolone resistance makes ciprofloxacin unreliable. Azithromycin alone does not reliably cure gonorrhea and fails to supply the recommended cephalosporin that treats it.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had seven outbreaks of genital herpes in the past year. Her partner has no history of herpes, and they want to reduce transmission and recurrences. What is the best management?
options: Episodic valacyclovir started only during outbreaks
Acyclovir cream applied to the skin daily
Daily suppressive valacyclovir, with condoms still used
Condoms alone, with no antiviral drug
items.explanation: Frequent recurrences and a susceptible partner are indications for daily suppressive therapy, which reduces recurrences and lowers, but does not eliminate, transmission, so condoms and disclosure still apply. Episodic treatment shortens outbreaks but does not suppress them. Topical antivirals have little effect. Condoms alone reduce risk but forgo a proven way to prevent most recurrences.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman discloses that her partner choked her last week. She is frightened but has not decided whether to leave him. What is the best response?
options: Advise that she must leave the relationship today
Call the police regardless of her wishes
Refer the couple for joint counseling sessions this month
Validate her, assess danger, and make a safety plan
items.explanation: The appropriate response is to believe and support her, assess immediate danger, build a safety plan, and connect her with advocacy services, while respecting her autonomy. Strangulation is a marker of high lethality risk, so the safety assessment is important. Pressuring her to leave or reporting against her wishes can erode trust and increase danger. Couples counseling is unsafe in the presence of abuse.

items.stem: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman with hypertension has three hours of fatigue, nausea, and jaw discomfort. She is diaphoretic and says she has no chest pain. What is the best next step?
options: Reassure her that acid reflux is the likely cause
Electrocardiogram and troponin measurement now
Arrange a stress test for next week
Give an antacid and reassess in the morning
items.explanation: Women with myocardial infarction often present with fatigue, nausea, dyspnea, or pain in the jaw, neck, or back rather than crushing chest pressure, so the absence of chest pain does not exclude it. An immediate electrocardiogram and troponin are required, with emergency transfer if abnormal. Reflux and delayed testing risk missing an infarction that needs urgent reperfusion.

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl received one dose of human papillomavirus vaccine at age 13 and never returned. She presents for a school physical. What is the correct action?
options: Give the second dose now; do not restart
Restart the entire series with three new doses
Give three doses starting today at 0, 2, and 6 months
No further dose, since one dose completes the series
items.explanation: She began the series before her 15th birthday, so a complete series needs only two doses at least 5 months apart. The interval has already passed, so the second dose now completes it. Vaccine series are never restarted because of delay. Three doses apply to starts at 15 or older or to immunocompromise. One dose is not considered a complete series.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has a painless, indurated 1 cm ulcer on the labia that appeared 2 weeks ago, with firm nontender inguinal nodes. Darkfield examination is unavailable. What is the most appropriate step today?
options: Prescribe oral acyclovir and wait for the culture result
Send syphilis serology and give benzathine penicillin G
Apply podofilox to the lesion twice daily
Treat only for chancroid and schedule review in a month
items.explanation: A single painless indurated ulcer with nontender nodes is a classic syphilitic chancre. Serology is sent, and treatment is started the same day when suspicion is high because follow-up may be lost. Herpes lesions are usually multiple and painful. Podofilox treats warts, not ulcers. Chancroid causes a painful ulcer with tender suppurative nodes and is uncommon in the United States.

items.stem: A 28-year-old nonpregnant woman has a Patient Health Questionnaire score of 14 and reports low mood for two months. She denies suicidal thoughts and has never had manic symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassurance and repeat screening in 12 months
A benzodiazepine for mood and sleep complaints
An antidepressant alone with no mention of therapy
Psychotherapy plus a serotonin reuptake inhibitor
items.explanation: A score of 10 or more suggests moderate depression that needs assessment and treatment. Combining psychotherapy with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor gives better results than either alone for moderate illness. Waiting a year ignores active symptoms. Benzodiazepines do not treat depression and carry dependence risk. Asking about prior mania, as done here, protects against provoking a manic switch.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has migraine with visual aura and asks to start a combined estrogen and progestin pill. Her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke. What is the best response?
options: Advise a non-estrogen method because of stroke risk
Prescribe the pill and add a daily aspirin
Prescribe the pill at the lowest estrogen dose
Prescribe it only if aura lasts under 10 minutes
items.explanation: Migraine with aura is an independent stroke risk factor, and estrogen-containing contraception adds to it, so these methods are not recommended regardless of dose or the length of the aura. Aspirin does not neutralize the risk of stroke. Progestin-only methods and the copper or levonorgestrel intrauterine devices are safe choices that can be offered instead.

items.stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman has a T-score of minus 2.7 at the lumbar spine on dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry. She has no fracture history, normal renal function, and no esophageal disease. Which is the best initial therapy?
options: Nasal calcitonin daily for several years
Vitamin D supplementation alone with annual rescanning
Weekly alendronate with calcium and vitamin D
Systemic estrogen as the preferred bone agent
items.explanation: Her T-score meets the threshold for osteoporosis, and oral bisphosphonates are first-line because they reduce vertebral and hip fractures at low cost. Calcitonin has weak fracture benefit and is rarely used. Vitamin D alone does not treat established osteoporosis. Estrogen protects bone but is not chosen primarily for that purpose when other agents are suitable.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman cares for her mother, who has dementia. She is exhausted, sleeps poorly, and has skipped her mammogram for two years. What is the best approach?
options: Prescribe a hypnotic and recheck her sleep next year
Screen for depression and arrange respite support
Advise her to place her mother in a facility
Defer all preventive care until caregiving ends
items.explanation: Caregiver strain contributes to depression, poor sleep, and missed preventive care, so the visit should screen for depression and connect her with respite and community support while also scheduling overdue screening. A hypnotic treats a symptom and ignores its cause. Telling her to relocate her mother is not the clinician's role. Deferring prevention compounds the harm to her own health.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is screened with the Patient Health Questionnaire and answers positively to thoughts of being better off dead. What is the most appropriate next step in the office?
options: Start an antidepressant and schedule review in six weeks
Give a handout about crisis lines and end the visit
Assess plan and intent, then make a safety plan
Repeat the questionnaire at the next annual visit
items.explanation: A positive item on suicidal thoughts requires an immediate direct assessment of ideation, plan, means, and intent, followed by a safety plan and a clear route to urgent care when risk is high. Starting medication alone without assessing risk is unsafe. A handout does not replace assessment, and delaying rescreening for a year leaves a patient at possible imminent risk without evaluation.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has dental erosion, parotid swelling, and calluses on her knuckles. Her potassium is 2.9 mEq/L and her body mass index is 22. She also reports depressed mood. Which medication should be avoided?
options: Fluoxetine, because of weight gain in bulimia
Sertraline, because of rebound binge eating
Escitalopram, because of prolonged potassium loss
Bupropion, because of seizure risk with purging
items.explanation: The findings indicate bulimia nervosa. Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, and purging with electrolyte disturbance compounds the risk, so it is contraindicated. Fluoxetine is actually the drug with evidence for reducing binge and purge frequency. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are not known to worsen binge eating or cause potassium loss. The hypokalemia should be corrected, and psychotherapy is the mainstay.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with cerebral palsy uses a wheelchair and cannot bear weight. She wants contraception that is safe and easy to use. Which method is the best choice?
options: A levonorgestrel intrauterine device
A combined oral contraceptive pill
A combined contraceptive vaginal ring
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate every three months
items.explanation: Estrogen-containing methods increase thrombosis risk, which is already higher in a patient who is immobile, so they are poor choices. Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate lowers bone density, a concern in someone who cannot bear weight. The levonorgestrel intrauterine device is highly effective, requires no daily action, and often reduces bleeding, which also helps with menstrual hygiene needs.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a sedentary job asks how much exercise she should aim for each week. What is the recommended target?
options: 75 minutes of moderate activity with no strengthening
150 minutes moderate activity plus strengthening twice
300 minutes of vigorous activity every week
10,000 steps daily with no other activity
items.explanation: Adults are advised to accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity weekly, with muscle-strengthening activities on two days. Seventy-five minutes is the minimum for vigorous activity and omits strengthening. Vigorous 300 minutes is far above the target for sedentary patients. A step count alone has no strengthening component and is not the standard recommendation.

items.stem: A 23-year-old transgender man has taken testosterone for three years and has had no menses for two. He has a cervix and has never had cervical screening. What is the best recommendation?
options: No screening, because amenorrhea means a low cervical cancer risk
Screening only if he reports sex with male partners
Screening only after he stops testosterone therapy
Cervical screening now, as for any patient with a cervix
items.explanation: Cervical cancer risk depends on the presence of a cervix and exposure to human papillomavirus, not on gender identity or menstrual status, so screening follows the same intervals as for other patients from age 21. Testosterone causes atrophy that can make samples unsatisfactory, and a smaller speculum, local estrogen, or self-collected testing helps. Stopping hormones is not required.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl asks her gynecologist for contraception and says she does not want her parents told. She is sexually active with a 15-year-old partner and reports no abuse. What is the best approach?
options: Call her parents first, because she is a minor
Defer contraception until a parent can attend
See her confidentially and explain the limits
Prescribe it only if she agrees to tell her parents
items.explanation: Minors in most states can consent to contraception, and confidentiality makes adolescents more likely to seek care. The clinician explains the limits, which are serious risk of harm and mandatory reports of abuse, and also asks how she wants billing and messages handled. Requiring parental involvement or delaying care increases the chance of unintended pregnancy and infection.

items.stem: A 29-week pregnant woman asks whether she needs any vaccines. Records show she received a tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis booster three years ago at a routine visit. What is the best recommendation?
options: Give tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccine now
Defer it because the booster three years ago still protects
Give tetanus and diphtheria toxoids without pertussis
Give it after delivery, before she leaves the hospital
items.explanation: One dose of the combined vaccine is recommended in every pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks, regardless of prior doses, because maternal antibody crosses the placenta and protects the newborn from pertussis. A previous booster does not substitute. Omitting pertussis defeats the purpose. Postpartum dosing gives the infant no passive antibody, so it is the wrong time to give it.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a history of preeclampsia, an LDL cholesterol of 140 mg/dL, no diabetes, and a calculated 10-year cardiovascular risk of 12 percent. What is the best therapy?
options: Fish oil capsules at a high daily dose
Extended-release niacin at bedtime
Lifestyle measures only for the next decade
A moderate-intensity statin
items.explanation: A statin is first-line for primary prevention in adults aged 40 to 75 with a risk factor and a 10-year risk of 10 percent or more, and preeclampsia history is a sex-specific risk enhancer that strengthens the case. Fish oil and niacin have not shown clear cardiovascular benefit over statins. Waiting ten years on lifestyle alone ignores her elevated calculated risk.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has several soft, flesh-colored papules on the vulva that she noticed a month ago. Examination suggests external genital warts and no other lesions. Which treatment is appropriate?
options: Oral valacyclovir taken once daily
Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G
Patient-applied imiquimod cream
Topical fluorouracil applied to the vulva
items.explanation: External warts are treated with patient-applied podofilox, imiquimod, or sinecatechins, or with clinician-applied cryotherapy, and recurrence is common because treatment removes lesions but not the virus. Valacyclovir treats herpes, and penicillin treats syphilis, neither of which causes warts. Topical fluorouracil is not a standard option on vulvar skin and can cause painful irritation and ulceration.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has fatigue, constipation, and heavier menses. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone is 12 mIU/L and free thyroxine is low. She is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Liothyronine alone, with no thyroxine component
Levothyroxine, repeat thyrotropin in 6 to 8 weeks
Radioactive iodine ablation of the gland
Observation with repeat thyroid testing in one year
items.explanation: An elevated thyrotropin with a low free thyroxine confirms overt hypothyroidism, which is treated with levothyroxine. Because the drug has a long half-life, the dose is adjusted by repeating thyrotropin after about 6 to 8 weeks. Liothyronine alone gives unstable levels. Radioactive iodine treats hyperthyroidism. Observing for a year leaves symptomatic disease untreated and her symptoms unaddressed.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a body mass index of 27 and no symptoms is seen for routine care. She has never had a test for diabetes. What is the best recommendation?
options: Screen with hemoglobin A1c or fasting glucose now
Wait until age 45 before testing glucose
Test only if she develops thirst and polyuria
Order a 100 g oral glucose load as the first test
items.explanation: Screening for abnormal glucose is recommended for adults aged 35 to 70 who have overweight or obesity, so she qualifies now, and a hemoglobin A1c or fasting glucose is the usual test. Waiting for symptoms or for age 45 delays diagnosis. A 100 g oral load is used in pregnancy testing, whereas a 75 g load is the nonpregnant diagnostic version and is not a first screening test.

items.stem: A 52-year-old healthy woman has never received a vaccine against shingles. She had chickenpox as a child and asks what is recommended. Which is the correct plan?
options: A single dose of live zoster vaccine now
Recombinant vaccine, two doses 2 to 6 months apart
Recombinant zoster vaccine as one dose only
Defer until age 65 because it is not approved earlier
items.explanation: Recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended as a two-dose series for adults from age 50, with the doses separated by 2 to 6 months. It is not live, and the live product is no longer used. One dose gives incomplete protection. There is no reason to wait until 65, since the benefit begins at 50 and a prior history of chickenpox does not remove the indication.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents 36 hours after an assault and requests emergency contraception. She is not on any medication and has a body mass index of 31. Which method is the most effective?
options: Copper intrauterine device
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally once
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally once
A combined pill taken in two divided doses
items.explanation: The copper intrauterine device is the most effective emergency method and can be placed up to 5 days after intercourse, with the added benefit of ongoing contraception. Ulipristal is more effective than levonorgestrel, particularly at higher body weight, and both are oral options if she declines the device. Combined pill regimens are less effective and cause more nausea.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman asks whether a daily low-dose aspirin would lower her chance of a heart attack. She has no cardiovascular disease, a low estimated 10-year risk, and a history of peptic ulcer bleeding. What is the best advice?
options: Start it, because it lowers cardiovascular risk in every woman
Start it, taken together with a proton pump inhibitor
Start it only during the luteal phase of each cycle
Not advised, since bleeding risk outweighs benefit
items.explanation: Routine aspirin for primary prevention is no longer advised, and for younger adults it is an individual decision that weighs bleeding risk. A prior ulcer bleed together with low cardiovascular risk tips the balance firmly against it. Adding acid suppression reduces but does not remove the danger. Timing aspirin to the cycle has no physiologic basis and does not change bleeding risk.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has a partner with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection and inconsistent condom use. She requests preexposure prophylaxis with daily emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. What must be confirmed first?
options: A normal CD4 count and a viral genotype
A negative pregnancy test and a bone density scan
A negative HIV test and adequate kidney function
A serum ferritin and a hepatitis A antibody level
items.explanation: Before starting, the clinician must document a negative infection status, because prophylaxis alone would breed resistance in an undetected infection, and check renal function because tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is nephrotoxic. Screening for hepatitis B is also done. CD4 counts and genotypes are used in treating established infection. Pregnancy does not preclude prophylaxis, and bone density scanning is not routine before starting.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a body mass index of 31 has no symptoms and no family history of cancer. She asks when she should begin screening for colorectal cancer. What is the best answer?
options: At age 50, using colonoscopy only
Now, at age 45, with stool testing or colonoscopy
At age 55, unless symptoms appear sooner
Only after a first-degree relative is diagnosed
items.explanation: Average-risk adults begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue to 75, and the choice includes stool-based tests, sigmoidoscopy, or colonoscopy according to patient preference and interval. Colonoscopy is not the only acceptable method. Waiting until 50 or 55 delays detection. Family history raises risk and moves the start earlier, but it is not required to begin screening.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has newly diagnosed endometrial cancer. Immunohistochemistry on the tumor shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 staining. Her brother had colon cancer at age 44. What is the best next step?
options: Testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants in the proband only
Repeat the tumor staining on a second block
Germline testing for Lynch syndrome after counseling
No further workup, because the cancer is sporadic
items.explanation: Loss of mismatch repair protein expression together with a young relative with colon cancer strongly suggests Lynch syndrome, so counseling and germline testing are needed, and the result also guides cascade testing of relatives. BRCA testing addresses a different syndrome. Repeating staining adds little. Calling the tumor sporadic ignores both the stain and the family history.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman attends the clinic with her husband, who insists on staying in the room. She has a healing bruise on her upper arm and seems anxious. What is the best way to screen for intimate partner violence?
options: See her alone, for example during urine collection
Ask the questions while her husband sits in the room
Ask the husband to explain the bruise first
Skip screening because the husband is present
items.explanation: Screening must occur in private, without a partner or relative present, since disclosure in front of the person causing harm is unsafe and unlikely. A routine step such as urine collection offers a natural reason to separate them without alerting him. Asking the husband to explain the injury can escalate danger. Skipping screening wastes a chance to help, and the clinician then documents findings and offers a safety plan if she discloses.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a diffuse maculopapular rash involving her palms and soles, along with mucous patches. Rapid plasma reagin titer is 1:64 and the treponemal test is reactive. She is not allergic to any drug. What is the treatment?
options: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units weekly for three doses
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
Azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly once
items.explanation: This is secondary syphilis, which is treated with a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G. Three weekly doses are reserved for late latent disease or disease of unknown duration. Doxycycline is an alternative only for penicillin allergy outside pregnancy. Azithromycin is no longer recommended because macrolide resistance is widespread and treatment failures have been reported in practice.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has stage 2 hypertension controlled on lisinopril and is planning conception within months. What is the best management of her medication?
options: Change to extended-release nifedipine before she conceives
Continue lisinopril until the pregnancy test is positive, then reduce the dose
Continue lisinopril and stop it only in the second trimester
Change to losartan, which is safe throughout pregnancy
items.explanation: Drugs that block the renin-angiotensin system are fetotoxic and should be replaced before conception or when pregnancy is first detected, using agents such as nifedipine or labetalol. Waiting for a positive test risks exposure during early organogenesis and later renal injury. Losartan belongs to the same harmful class, so changing to it solves nothing for the fetus.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with opioid use disorder asks for help. She uses daily and has failed two attempts at stopping on her own. Which plan is best?
options: A two-week taper with clonidine and counseling alone
Buprenorphine maintenance plus a naloxone kit
Detoxification followed by weekly group meetings only
Naltrexone started while she is still using opioids
items.explanation: Medication with buprenorphine or methadone lowers mortality and relapse, is continued without a rapid taper, and is paired with naloxone for overdose rescue. Short tapers and detoxification alone have high relapse and raise overdose risk because tolerance falls. Naltrexone requires a period without any opioids first, and starting it during ongoing use can precipitate acute withdrawal.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has a confirmed pathogenic MLH1 variant. Her mother had endometrial cancer. When should colonoscopic surveillance be performed?
options: Every 10 years, starting at the average-risk age of 45
Every 5 years, starting at age 50
Sigmoidoscopy every 5 years from age 40
Every 1 to 2 years, starting at age 20 to 25
items.explanation: Lynch syndrome carries a very high colorectal cancer risk and cancers arise at young ages, so colonoscopy starts in the early twenties and repeats every 1 to 2 years. Average-risk schedules begin at 45 and use long intervals. Sigmoidoscopy misses right-sided lesions, which are typical of Lynch cancers. Surveillance should therefore not follow the population plan.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought in by an older man who answers all questions for her. She has no identification, gives an inconsistent history, and has her third sexually transmitted infection this year. What is the best approach?
options: Confront the man about the situation in the room
Call the police immediately without speaking to her
Interview her alone and offer confidential hotline information
Treat the infection and document nothing else
items.explanation: Controlled movement, no identification, an inconsistent history, and repeated infections raise concern for trafficking. The clinician should find a way to speak with her privately, treat the infection, and offer a hotline and resources without endangering her. Confronting the man could escalate harm. Reporting without her involvement ignores her safety and wishes, and ignoring the pattern misses a chance to help.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman at high risk of HIV exposure has trouble taking daily pills and wants a long-acting prevention option. Which choice is appropriate?
options: Daily emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide
Cabotegravir injections given every 2 months
Doxycycline taken after sexual exposure
A single ceftriaxone injection before intercourse
items.explanation: Long-acting injectable cabotegravir every 2 months is an approved prophylaxis option, and lenacapavir every 6 months is another. Tenofovir alafenamide with emtricitabine was not studied for receptive vaginal sex and is not preferred in women. Doxycycline after sex lowers bacterial infections in selected groups and does not prevent HIV. Ceftriaxone has no role in preventing viral infection.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman is treated for gonorrhea. She reports sex with one male partner, the last encounter 3 weeks ago, and says he lives out of state and will not attend a clinic. What is the best way to manage her partner?
options: Offer expedited partner therapy for him to take
Tell her to wait until he has symptoms
Treat him only after his own positive test
Notify him when she returns for her three-month retest
items.explanation: Partners with sexual contact in the 60 days before diagnosis should be evaluated and treated, and expedited partner therapy, which gives the patient medication or a prescription for the partner, is allowed in most states for heterosexual partners. Waiting for symptoms is a mistake because many infections are silent. Requiring a positive test or delaying until retesting allows reinfection and ongoing spread.

items.stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman smokes daily, has a body mass index of 19, and her mother had a hip fracture at age 70. She has never had bone testing. What is the best recommendation?
options: Wait until age 65 for the first scan
Measure a serum vitamin D level instead
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry now
Obtain a lateral spine radiograph every year
items.explanation: Postmenopausal women younger than 65 with risk factors such as low body weight, smoking, and a parent with hip fracture should be screened with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry. Waiting until 65 would miss a high-risk window. A vitamin D level does not measure fracture risk. Plain radiographs are insensitive for bone loss until it is advanced, so they are not a screening method.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman records daily symptom ratings for two cycles. Marked irritability, tearfulness, and anxiety begin about 6 days before menses, resolve within 3 days of bleeding, and cost her several workdays. What is the best initial treatment?
options: A benzodiazepine taken every evening of the cycle
Progesterone cream applied during the luteal phase
A gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist without add-back
A serotonin reuptake inhibitor, daily or luteal only
items.explanation: Her pattern confirms premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first-line and work with either schedule. Benzodiazepines risk dependence and are not recommended as primary therapy. Topical progesterone has no proven benefit over placebo. A gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist is reserved for refractory disease and needs add-back therapy to protect bone and limit menopausal symptoms.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa has a heart rate of 38 beats per minute, orthostatic dizziness, and a body mass index of 15. What is the most appropriate setting for care?
options: Hospital admission with monitored refeeding
Outpatient therapy with weekly weights
Start fluoxetine and discharge today
An oral contraceptive to restore her menses
items.explanation: Severe bradycardia, orthostasis, and marked underweight indicate medical instability, which requires admission, and refeeding is monitored for hypophosphatemia. Outpatient therapy is only appropriate when she is stable. Fluoxetine has little effect on anorexia at low weight. A contraceptive produces withdrawal bleeding without restoring bone or weight, and weight restoration is the actual treatment of the amenorrhea.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with long-standing heavy menses reports fatigue. Her hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 74 fL, and ferritin is 8 ng/mL. She has no gastrointestinal symptoms. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Intramuscular vitamin B12 monthly
Red cell transfusion in the clinic this week
Folic acid 1 mg daily for three months
Oral iron once daily or on alternate days
items.explanation: The microcytosis and very low ferritin establish iron deficiency from menstrual loss. Oral iron, taken once daily or every other day to improve absorption, corrects it, and the bleeding source is also addressed. Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency cause macrocytosis. Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic instability or severe anemia, which this stable patient does not have. Intravenous iron is used for intolerance or poor absorption.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with no symptoms requests a combined oral contraceptive. Her blood pressure is normal, and her last cervical screening was normal one year ago. What is the best approach?
options: Perform a bimanual examination before prescribing
Perform a speculum examination before prescribing
Prescribe it today; a pelvic examination is not required
Delay the prescription until a pelvic examination is done
items.explanation: Contraception can be prescribed after a history and blood pressure check, and a pelvic examination is not needed for an asymptomatic patient. Requiring any internal examination as a precondition creates a barrier to care and has no safety benefit. Her cervical screening is not due, and cervical samples are never a prerequisite for starting a hormonal method.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with urgency incontinence takes oxybutynin and her family reports new forgetfulness and a recent fall. Which change is most appropriate?
options: Increase the oxybutynin dose for better bladder control
Stop the anticholinergic; start bladder training
Add a second anticholinergic with less sedation
Continue it and add a nightly sedative
items.explanation: Anticholinergic bladder drugs impair cognition and increase falls in older adults, and geriatric criteria list them as drugs to avoid. Stopping the drug and starting behavioral measures, with a beta-3 agonist if medication is still needed, addresses both problems. Raising the dose or adding another anticholinergic worsens confusion. A sedative adds further fall risk and more confusion.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl, menarche at 12, has had only three menses in the past year, with intervals of up to 100 days. She is not sexually active, and she is not on medication. What is the best approach?
options: Test for pregnancy, thyroid, prolactin, and androgens
Reassure her that irregularity is normal for three years
Start a combined pill now, without any prior testing
Order brain magnetic resonance imaging as the first step
items.explanation: A cycle longer than 90 days is outside the normal range at any gynecologic age and calls for evaluation, starting with a pregnancy test and measures such as thyrotropin, prolactin, and androgens. Reassurance fits cycles up to 45 days in an adolescent. Starting hormones without a diagnosis may mask polycystic ovary syndrome or other causes. Imaging is reserved for specific neurologic findings.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman asks whether she must keep having cervical screening. She has had three consecutive normal cytology results, the last two years ago, and no history of abnormal findings or treatment. What should be advised?
options: Continue cytology every year for life
Continue testing every three years until age 80
Do one more test, then stop only after a colposcopy
Stop screening, since prior results are adequate
items.explanation: Women 65 or older with adequate negative screening, meaning three consecutive normal cytology results or two normal co-tests within the past 10 years, with the most recent within 5 years, and no history of high-grade precancer may stop. Her history satisfies those criteria. Colposcopy is for abnormal results, and routine annual testing after age 65 provides no added benefit.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman comes for a well-woman visit. She smoked one and a half packs daily for 20 years and quit 8 years ago. She has no cough, weight loss, or hemoptysis, and she is otherwise healthy. Which screening test is indicated?
options: Chest radiography every year until age 75
Sputum cytology twice a year for five years
Annual low-dose computed tomography of the chest
No screening, because she has no symptoms now
items.explanation: She has 30 pack-years and quit within the past 15 years, and she is between 50 and 80, so she meets criteria for annual low-dose computed tomography. Chest radiography has not been shown to lower lung cancer mortality, and sputum cytology is not a screening tool. Absence of symptoms is the point of screening, so waiting for symptoms defeats its purpose.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has never received human papillomavirus vaccine and asks whether it is worthwhile at her age. She is not pregnant. What is the best response?
options: It is not indicated for anyone older than 26
It is given only after a negative HPV test
It is given only if she has never had sex
It may be given through shared decision making with the clinician
items.explanation: Catch-up vaccination is recommended through age 26, and for adults aged 27 to 45 the decision is shared between patient and clinician, because the benefit is smaller but real for those who may meet new types. A prior test or sexual history does not exclude her, since the vaccine protects against types she may not have acquired. The vaccine is not given in pregnancy.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 29 weeks asks about vaccination. She received a tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis booster three years ago. What is the best recommendation?
options: Defer Tdap until after delivery
Give Tdap now, since it is recommended in every pregnancy
Skip it because she was vaccinated within five years
Give tetanus and diphtheria toxoid without pertussis
items.explanation: Tdap is recommended during every pregnancy, preferably between 27 and 36 weeks, regardless of prior vaccination, so that maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn from pertussis. Postpartum dosing misses that protection. A recent booster does not remove the indication. Tetanus and diphtheria toxoid alone omits pertussis, which is the reason for the dose.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman whose mother had breast cancer at age 61 asks whether she needs genetic testing. She has no personal cancer history, and no other relatives have had breast, ovarian, or related cancers. What is the best answer?
options: Testing is not indicated on this history alone
Testing is indicated because a first-degree relative has cancer
She should begin annual breast magnetic resonance imaging
She should have BRCA testing and tubal removal at 40
items.explanation: A single relative diagnosed after menopause, without ovarian cancer, male breast cancer, triple-negative disease, or known ancestry risk, does not meet usual referral criteria, and a brief familial risk tool would be negative. Routine counseling of women with negative screens is not recommended. Magnetic resonance imaging is advised at 20 percent or higher lifetime risk, and surgery is premature.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman takes diphenhydramine nightly for insomnia and has recently been confused and unsteady. What is the best management?
options: Double the dose for more reliable sleep
Switch to a nightly sedative-hypnotic instead
Stop the drug and start cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia
Continue it and add a second sleep aid
items.explanation: Sedating antihistamines have anticholinergic effects that cause confusion and falls in older adults and appear on geriatric lists of drugs to avoid. Cognitive behavioral therapy is the first-line treatment for insomnia and avoids these risks. Raising the dose or adding a second sedating drug worsens cognition. Sedative-hypnotics are similarly associated with falls and fractures in this age group.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman has a body mass index of 37 and type 2 diabetes controlled poorly on medication, despite a year of supervised lifestyle programs. She asks about surgical options. What is the best response?
options: She must reach a body mass index of 40 before referral
She is a candidate for referral for bariatric surgery
She should repeat the lifestyle program for a further year
Surgery is contraindicated while she has diabetes
items.explanation: Bariatric surgery is offered for a body mass index of 40 or more, or 35 or more with a weight-related condition such as diabetes, and she meets the second criterion and has failed lifestyle therapy. Requiring a body mass index of 40 would apply only to those without comorbidity. Diabetes is an indication for surgery, not a contraindication, and it often improves afterward.

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl with HIV infection has never received human papillomavirus vaccine. How many doses does she need to complete the series?
options: Two doses at least 5 months apart
One dose with a booster later
None because she is immunocompromised
Three doses at 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months
items.explanation: Immunocompromised persons, including those with HIV, need a three-dose human papillomavirus series regardless of age at the start, given at 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months. The two-dose schedule applies only to immunocompetent people who start before age 15. A single dose is not an approved schedule here. Immunosuppression is not a contraindication, because the vaccine is not live.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has never been tested for hepatitis C. She has no risk factors, is not pregnant, and has normal liver enzymes. What is the recommendation?
options: Test once now: antibody, then reflex RNA
Test only if she ever reports injection drug use
Test every year for the rest of her adult life
Test only if she becomes pregnant in the future
items.explanation: Every adult is screened once for hepatitis C regardless of risk, because many infections are silent and curative treatment is available. A positive antibody test is followed by confirmatory RNA testing. Limiting screening to injection drug use misses many infections. Annual testing is for ongoing risk, and waiting for pregnancy delays diagnosis, although testing is also repeated in each pregnancy.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has taken denosumab for four years for osteoporosis and wants to stop because of cost. Which is the best advice?
options: Stop now and rely on calcium and vitamin D alone
Follow the last dose with a bisphosphonate
Stop now and recheck density in five years
Take a two-year drug holiday before any new agent
items.explanation: Stopping denosumab causes rapid bone loss and rebound vertebral fractures, so a follow-on agent, usually a bisphosphonate, must be given when it is discontinued. Calcium and vitamin D alone cannot prevent the rebound. Waiting years to recheck leaves the fracture window uncovered. A drug holiday is a concept for bisphosphonates, whose effect persists in bone, and not for denosumab.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl has crampy lower abdominal pain for the first two days of each period since menarche 18 months ago. Pelvic examination findings are normal and she is not sexually active. What is the best first treatment?
options: Diagnostic laparoscopy to look for endometriosis
A gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist for three months
A nonsteroidal drug begun when bleeding starts
A short course of an opioid analgesic each cycle
items.explanation: The timing and normal examination fit primary dysmenorrhea, which is driven by prostaglandins, so a nonsteroidal drug begun at or just before bleeding is first-line. Laparoscopy is considered only after failed medical therapy. A gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist is too aggressive for a first step in an adolescent. Opioids are not appropriate for this recurring, self-limited pain.

items.stem: A 49-year-old asymptomatic woman has a hemoglobin A1c of 6.7 percent on routine testing. She has no other glucose results. What is the best next step?
options: Start metformin and recheck in six months
Diagnose prediabetes and counsel on lifestyle
Order a 100 g oral glucose tolerance test
Repeat A1c or fasting glucose to confirm the diagnosis
items.explanation: A single abnormal result in an asymptomatic patient is confirmed with a repeat test, since diabetes is diagnosed by an A1c of 6.5 percent or more or a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or more. Starting a drug before confirmation is premature. Her value is above the prediabetes range, so that label is wrong. A 100 g load is a pregnancy test, and a 75 g load would be the nonpregnant version.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman considering genetic testing says she fears it could raise her life insurance rates. Which statement about federal protection is accurate?
options: It covers every type of insurance, life insurance included
It covers life and disability insurance but not health coverage
It covers health insurance, but not life insurance
It covers employment only and has no insurance provisions
items.explanation: The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act bars discrimination in health insurance and employment, but it does not cover life, disability, or long-term care insurance, a gap that patients should hear about before testing. Claiming complete protection overstates the law. Reversing the coverage inverts it, since health insurance is protected. Insurance provisions are in fact a central part of the statute.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents on day 6 of painful genital vesicles and ulcers, with dysuria and tender inguinal nodes. She has never had similar lesions. Polymerase chain reaction of lesion fluid is positive for herpes simplex virus type 2. What is the best treatment?
options: Acyclovir cream applied to lesions until they heal
Valacyclovir by mouth for 7 to 10 days
Valacyclovir by mouth for 3 days
No antiviral until type-specific serology returns
items.explanation: A first clinical episode can be severe and prolonged, so oral antiviral therapy is given for 7 to 10 days even when the patient presents late. Topical antivirals add little and do not treat systemic symptoms. A three-day course is for recurrences. Waiting for serology delays care and is unnecessary once a lesion test has confirmed the diagnosis.

items.stem: The parents of a 19-year-old woman with a moderate intellectual disability ask the gynecologist to sterilize her. She has not asked for it. What is the correct response?
options: Seek her supported consent or use the legal process
Proceed because both of her parents have requested it
Proceed if she seems to agree when it is explained
Perform it during another planned procedure
items.explanation: Sterilization is never performed without the patient's own informed consent or the legal process that the state requires, and capacity is judged for the specific decision with supported decision making. Parental request alone is not valid consent for an adult. Apparent assent does not meet the standard. Adding it to another surgery would circumvent consent entirely.
